stem: During in-hospital CPR on an adult of average build, which combination of chest compression depth and rate is recommended?

options.A: Depth 5–6 cm at 80–100 compressions/min
options.B: Depth 6–8 cm at 120–140 compressions/min
options.C: Depth 3–4 cm at 100–120 compressions/min
options.D: Depth 4–5 cm at 60–80 compressions/min
options.E: Depth 5–6 cm at 100–120 compressions/min

explanation: ERC 2021 and AHA 2020 guidelines both recommend a compression depth of about 5 cm but not more than 6 cm, a rate of 100–120/min, full chest recoil and minimal interruptions. Excessive depth (>6 cm) increases injury, and rates above 120/min reduce depth and diastolic filling time.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]; Panchal et al. 2020 (AHA adult BLS/ALS) [158]

stem: A 62-year-old man on a cardiology ward has a witnessed VF arrest. He remains in VF after the third shock, and IV access is established. In addition to continuing CPR, which drug therapy is now indicated?

options.A: Adrenaline 3 mg IV and magnesium 2 g IV
options.B: Lidocaine 1 mg/kg IV and vasopressin 40 units IV
options.C: Adrenaline 1 mg IV and amiodarone 300 mg IV
options.D: Amiodarone 150 mg IV only
options.E: Adrenaline 1 mg IV only; amiodarone after the fifth shock

explanation: In shockable rhythms, ERC guidance gives adrenaline 1 mg and amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock, then adrenaline every 3–5 minutes (alternate cycles). A further 150 mg of amiodarone is given after the fifth shock. Lidocaine is an alternative only when amiodarone is unavailable; vasopressin and high-dose adrenaline are not recommended.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: In refractory VF, after amiodarone 300 mg has already been given after the third shock, when is the second (150 mg) amiodarone dose recommended?

options.A: Only after 20 minutes of resuscitation
options.B: After the fifth shock
options.C: It is not recommended; switch to lidocaine instead
options.D: After the fourth shock
options.E: After the sixth shock

explanation: ERC 2021 recommends amiodarone 300 mg after three defibrillation attempts and a further 150 mg after five defibrillation attempts. Lidocaine (1 mg/kg) is an alternative if amiodarone is unavailable, not a mandatory switch.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: A 70-year-old woman is found in asystole on the ward. CPR is started and IV access is obtained. When should the first dose of adrenaline be given?

options.A: After 10 minutes if there is no return of spontaneous circulation
options.B: Only after a definitive airway has been secured
options.C: After the second rhythm check
options.D: After 3 cycles of CPR, at the same time as amiodarone
options.E: As soon as IV or IO access is obtained

explanation: In non-shockable rhythms (PEA/asystole), adrenaline 1 mg should be given as soon as vascular access is achieved and repeated every 3–5 minutes. Delaying adrenaline in non-shockable arrest is associated with worse outcomes, and airway management should not delay drug administration.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: Minutes after insertion of a left subclavian central venous catheter, a ventilated patient develops PEA. Peak airway pressure has risen sharply, and breath sounds are absent on the left. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Adrenaline 1 mg IV and await chest radiograph confirmation before any intervention
options.B: Increase PEEP to recruit the collapsed lung
options.C: Pericardiocentesis
options.D: Administer thrombolysis for suspected pulmonary embolism
options.E: Immediate left needle or finger thoracostomy while continuing CPR

explanation: Tension pneumothorax is one of the reversible causes (4 Hs and 4 Ts) and is a clinical diagnosis. Decompression should not wait for imaging; in ventilated patients, finger thoracostomy is effective. Increasing PEEP would worsen the tension physiology.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: A haemodialysis patient who missed two sessions has a cardiac arrest. A pre-arrest ECG showed a sine-wave pattern and the point-of-care potassium is 8.4 mmol/L. In addition to ALS, what is the most appropriate first-line specific treatment?

options.A: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g orally
options.B: Salbutamol 10 mg nebulised
options.C: Calcium chloride 10% 10 mL by rapid IV bolus
options.D: Sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 200 mL over 30 minutes
options.E: Furosemide 80 mg IV

explanation: In hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest, ERC recommends calcium chloride 10% 10 mL IV to stabilise the myocardium, plus insulin–glucose (10 units with 25 g glucose), consideration of bicarbonate, and dialysis for refractory cases. Nebulised salbutamol and binders are not practical during CPR.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: A patient 6 hours after coronary artery bypass grafting develops monitored VF in the cardiac ICU, with defibrillator pads already attached. What is the recommended initial management?

options.A: Adrenaline 1 mg IV followed by a single shock
options.B: Amiodarone 300 mg IV followed by a single shock
options.C: Emergency resternotomy before any defibrillation attempt
options.D: Up to three rapid successive (stacked) shocks before chest compressions
options.E: Immediate external chest compressions for 2 minutes before attempting any shock

explanation: After cardiac surgery, and in other monitored witnessed VF/pVT with a defibrillator immediately available, three stacked shocks are recommended before external compressions. Full-dose adrenaline is avoided early because of the risk of rebound hypertension; resternotomy is considered if there is no ROSC within about 5 minutes.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: During CPR of an intubated patient, end-tidal CO2 suddenly rises from 15 mmHg to 42 mmHg during continuous compressions. What does this most likely indicate?

options.A: Development of tension pneumothorax
options.B: Rescuer fatigue with shallower compressions
options.C: Return of spontaneous circulation
options.D: Oesophageal intubation
options.E: Accidental extubation

explanation: Waveform capnography confirms tracheal tube placement, monitors CPR quality, and an abrupt sustained rise in ETCO2 during CPR is an early indicator of ROSC. Oesophageal intubation, extubation and worsening compressions would all cause ETCO2 to fall, not rise.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: Once a tracheal tube is placed during cardiac arrest, how should ventilation be delivered?

options.A: About 10 breaths/min with continuous chest compressions
options.B: No ventilation until ROSC; passive oxygenation only
options.C: 2 breaths after every 30 compressions with compression pauses
options.D: 20 breaths/min to correct acidosis
options.E: 6 breaths/min with tidal volume of 15 mL/kg

explanation: Once an advanced airway is in place, compressions continue uninterrupted and ventilation is given at about 10 breaths/min, each over about 1 second with visible chest rise. Hyperventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, reduces venous return and coronary perfusion.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]; Panchal et al. 2020 (AHA adult BLS/ALS) [158]

stem: A woman at 32 weeks' gestation has a cardiac arrest in the delivery suite. High-quality CPR with manual left uterine displacement is in progress. If there is no ROSC, when should resuscitative hysterotomy (perimortem caesarean delivery) be performed?

options.A: Only after transfer to the main operating theatre
options.B: Begun by about 4 minutes after arrest to achieve delivery by 5 minutes
options.C: Not indicated because the fetus is viable and should be delivered after ROSC
options.D: Only if fetal heart sounds are present on Doppler
options.E: Only after 20 minutes of unsuccessful resuscitation

explanation: When the uterus is at or above the umbilicus (about 20 weeks), aortocaval compression impairs CPR. Resuscitative hysterotomy should be started about 4 minutes after arrest, aiming for delivery within 5 minutes, primarily to improve maternal resuscitation; it should be performed at the bedside.
referenceText: Jeejeebhoy et al. 2015 (AHA cardiac arrest in pregnancy) [103]; Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: A patient receiving IV haloperidol and azithromycin develops recurrent self-terminating polymorphic VT with a long QT on ECG. Serum K+ is 3.3 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate first drug treatment?

options.A: Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 10 minutes
options.B: Sotalol 1.5 mg/kg IV
options.C: Procainamide 15 mg/kg IV
options.D: Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20 minutes, then 900 mg over 24 hours
options.E: Flecainide 2 mg/kg IV

explanation: Torsades de pointes is treated by stopping QT-prolonging drugs, giving IV magnesium (2 g), and correcting potassium to the high-normal range. Amiodarone, procainamide and sotalol prolong the QT interval and may worsen torsades; isoprenaline or overdrive pacing are options for recurrence.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]; Zeppenfeld et al. 2022 (ESC ventricular arrhythmias) [246]

stem: After ROSC from out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, a patient is ventilated in the ICU. Which set of targets is recommended?

options.A: SpO2 94–98%, PaCO2 25–30 mmHg, MAP above 100 mmHg
options.B: SpO2 94–98%, normocapnia, MAP above 60–65 mmHg
options.C: SpO2 88–92%, PaCO2 50–55 mmHg, MAP above 55 mmHg
options.D: PaO2 above 300 mmHg, normocapnia, MAP above 90 mmHg
options.E: SpO2 100% with FiO2 1.0 for 24 hours, PaCO2 30 mmHg

explanation: The ERC–ESICM 2025 post-resuscitation guidelines recommend titrating oxygen to SpO2 94–98% (avoiding hypoxaemia, PaO2 below 8 kPa/60 mmHg, and hyperoxaemia), targeting normocapnia (PaCO2 4.7–6.0 kPa, 35–45 mmHg), and avoiding hypotension with a MAP above 60–65 mmHg (the 2021 version stated above 65 mmHg). Hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction and may worsen brain injury.
referenceText: Nolan et al. 2021 (ERC–ESICM post-resuscitation care) [153]; ERC–ESICM 2025 post-resuscitation care [249]
updateNote: ERC–ESICM 2025: MAP target is now >60–65 mmHg (was >65 mmHg).

stem: A comatose survivor of out-of-hospital VF arrest is admitted to ICU. Based on the TTM2 trial and the 2025 ERC–ESICM guidance, what is the most appropriate temperature strategy?

options.A: Actively prevent fever, targeting 37.5 °C or less, for 36–72 hours
options.B: Prophylactic paracetamol only, with cooling devices contraindicated
options.C: Induce hypothermia to 33 °C for 24 hours in all patients
options.D: Induce hypothermia to 32 °C for 72 hours
options.E: No temperature monitoring is required if the patient is normothermic on arrival

explanation: TTM2 found no difference in mortality or functional outcome between targeted hypothermia at 33 °C and normothermia with early treatment of fever. ERC–ESICM 2025 suggest actively preventing fever by targeting a temperature of 37.5 °C or less in patients who remain comatose after ROSC (weak recommendation, low certainty), for 36–72 hours (good practice statement), with continuous core temperature monitoring. Patients with mild hypothermia (32–36 °C) after ROSC should not be actively rewarmed. (ERC–ESICM 2021 had defined fever as above 37.7 °C and advised prevention for at least 72 hours.)
referenceText: Dankiewicz et al. 2021 (TTM2) [46]; Nolan et al. 2021 (ERC–ESICM post-resuscitation care) [153]; ERC–ESICM 2025 post-resuscitation care [249]
updateNote: ERC–ESICM 2025: fever prevention target ≤37.5 °C for 36–72 h (was >37.7 °C for ≥72 h).

stem: According to ERC–ESICM 2025, in a patient who is not obeying commands (Glasgow motor score below 6) at 72 hours or later after ROSC and has no confounders, which finding is one of the predictors of poor neurological outcome?

options.A: Unilaterally absent corneal reflex at 24 hours
options.B: Bilaterally absent N20 waves on SSEP
options.C: Myoclonus lasting 10 minutes on day 1
options.D: Neuron-specific enolase of 20 µg/L at 48 hours
options.E: A single episode of hypotension after ROSC

explanation: ERC–ESICM 2025 advise considering prognostication in patients who are not awake and obeying commands (GCS motor score below 6) at 72 h or later after ROSC (the 2021 algorithm applied it to motor score 3 or less). In an unconscious patient at ≥72 h without confounders, poor outcome is likely when two or more predictors are present: bilaterally absent pupillary and corneal reflexes at ≥72 h, bilaterally absent N20 SSEP waves at ≥24 h, highly malignant EEG after 24 h, NSE above 60 µg/L at 48 h and/or 72 h, status myoclonus within 72 h, and extensive diffuse anoxic injury on CT/MRI.
referenceText: Nolan et al. 2021 (ERC–ESICM post-resuscitation care) [153]; ERC–ESICM 2025 post-resuscitation care [249]
updateNote: ERC–ESICM 2025: prognostication applies when GCS motor <6 at ≥72 h; SSEP valid from 24 h.

stem: A comatose patient remains on propofol and fentanyl infusions on day 3 after cardiac arrest. Neuron-specific enolase at 72 hours is 85 µg/L. What is the most important next step before concluding that the prognosis is poor?

options.A: Withdraw life-sustaining treatment now, because an NSE above 60 µg/L is diagnostic on its own
options.B: Exclude confounders such as sedation, then apply multimodal assessment with two or more predictors
options.C: Perform an apnoea test
options.D: Repeat NSE daily and defer all decisions until it falls below 17 µg/L
options.E: Wait for 6 months before any prognostic decision

explanation: Prognostication should be multimodal and is considered at 72 hours or later after ROSC in patients not obeying commands (GCS motor score below 6), after excluding confounders such as sedatives, neuromuscular blockers, hypothermia, severe hypotension and metabolic derangements. A single elevated biomarker is not sufficient; the ERC–ESICM 2025 algorithm requires two or more predictors (NSE above 60 µg/L at 48 h and/or 72 h is one; bilaterally absent N20 SSEP waves can be used from 24 h). Haemolysis can also falsely elevate NSE.
referenceText: Nolan et al. 2021 (ERC–ESICM post-resuscitation care) [153]; ERC–ESICM 2025 post-resuscitation care [249]
updateNote: ERC–ESICM 2025 prognostication criteria (GCS motor <6 at ≥72 h; SSEP from 24 h).

stem: After ROSC from out-of-hospital VF arrest, a 55-year-old man has an ECG showing 3 mm ST elevation in leads V2–V5. He is haemodynamically stable on low-dose noradrenaline. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Thrombolysis followed by elective angiography at 2 weeks
options.B: Delayed angiography after neurological recovery is confirmed
options.C: Medical therapy only because he is comatose
options.D: CT coronary angiography at 72 hours
options.E: Emergency coronary angiography with primary PCI if indicated

explanation: Patients with ST elevation after ROSC should undergo emergency coronary angiography. In patients without ST elevation, trials such as COACT and TOMAHAWK did not show benefit from routine immediate angiography, so it is considered selectively based on suspected coronary cause and haemodynamic or electrical instability.
referenceText: Nolan et al. 2021 (ERC–ESICM post-resuscitation care) [153]; Byrne et al. 2023 (ESC acute coronary syndromes) [29]

stem: A haemodynamically stable patient regains ROSC after VF arrest. The post-ROSC ECG shows no ST elevation, and there is no ongoing ischaemia or electrical instability. Which strategy regarding coronary angiography is supported by current evidence?

options.A: Thrombolysis before any angiography
options.B: Angiography only after a 6-month functional assessment
options.C: Coronary angiography is contraindicated after cardiac arrest
options.D: Delayed or selective angiography rather than routine emergency angiography
options.E: Emergency coronary angiography within 2 hours in all such resuscitated patients

explanation: Randomised trials (COACT, TOMAHAWK) found no survival benefit from routine immediate angiography in resuscitated patients without ST elevation. Emergency angiography is reserved for those with high suspicion of ongoing coronary occlusion, cardiogenic shock or recurrent arrhythmias.
referenceText: Lemkes et al. 2019 (COACT) [127]; Desch et al. 2021 (TOMAHAWK) [53]; Nolan et al. 2021 (ERC–ESICM post-resuscitation care) [153]

stem: During a femoral nerve block with bupivacaine, a patient seizes and then develops pulseless VT. In addition to standard ALS, what specific therapy is indicated?

options.A: Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV
options.B: Flumazenil 0.5 mg IV
options.C: 20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus followed by an infusion
options.D: Sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 50 mL bolus as the definitive therapy
options.E: Naloxone 2 mg IV

explanation: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity causing arrest is treated with standard ALS and intravenous 20% lipid emulsion (1.5 mL/kg bolus, then 15 mL/kg/h infusion; repeat boluses as needed). CPR may need to be prolonged; extracorporeal support can be considered. Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]; Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

stem: A man rescued from the sea is in VF with a core temperature of 27 °C. Three shocks have been delivered without success. What is the recommended approach to drugs and further shocks?

options.A: Give adrenaline every 3–5 minutes and shock every 2 minutes as usual
options.B: Stop CPR because survival is unlikely below 28 °C
options.C: Withhold adrenaline and further shocks until core temperature exceeds 30 °C; continue CPR and rewarming
options.D: Give adrenaline every 1–2 minutes and shock after every cycle, because drug clearance increases in hypothermia
options.E: Give amiodarone 300 mg and adrenaline 1 mg immediately

explanation: In hypothermic arrest below 30 °C, the ERC recommends withholding adrenaline and limiting to three shocks until core temperature exceeds 30 °C; between 30 and 35 °C, the adrenaline interval is doubled to 6–10 minutes. Extracorporeal rewarming (ECLS) is preferred for hypothermic arrest, and good outcomes are possible after prolonged CPR.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]; Brown et al. 2012 (accidental hypothermia) [27]

stem: A young man is pulled unresponsive from a swimming pool and is not breathing normally. How should basic life support begin?

options.A: Perform abdominal thrusts to drain water from the lungs
options.B: Apply cervical collar and wait for spinal immobilisation before CPR
options.C: Give 2 rescue breaths and then compression-only CPR
options.D: Start with 30 chest compressions before any ventilation
options.E: Give 5 initial rescue breaths before starting chest compressions

explanation: Drowning causes hypoxic arrest, so oxygenation is the priority; the ERC recommends 5 initial rescue breaths (ideally with supplemental oxygen) followed by 30:2 CPR. Abdominal thrusts are not recommended to remove water, and routine spinal immobilisation is unnecessary unless there are signs of trauma.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]; Szpilman et al. 2012 (drowning) [204]

stem: A heart-transplant recipient develops symptomatic sinus bradycardia at 35 beats/min with hypotension. Which statement about first-line drug therapy is correct?

options.A: Adenosine is the treatment of choice
options.B: Verapamil should be given to restore conduction through the transplanted atrioventricular node
options.C: Intravenous digoxin should be loaded
options.D: Atropine 3 mg IV is the first choice, because vagal tone is preserved and dominant after cardiac transplantation
options.E: Atropine is likely to be ineffective in the denervated heart; use isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion

explanation: Atropine acts by vagal blockade and is unlikely to work in denervated transplanted hearts, and paradoxical high-degree AV block has been described. Isoprenaline or adrenaline infusions, aminophylline, or pacing are preferred in these patients.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: A patient with a broad-complex tachycardia at 190/min is confused with a systolic blood pressure of 70 mmHg. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Unsynchronised shock at 360 J
options.B: Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 60 minutes, then reassess before any shock
options.C: Verapamil 5 mg IV
options.D: Synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation or anaesthesia
options.E: Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV bolus

explanation: Tachyarrhythmia with adverse features (shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia or heart failure) is treated with synchronised cardioversion, up to three attempts, then amiodarone 300 mg over 10–20 minutes and repeat shocks. Unsynchronised shocks are for pulseless rhythms; verapamil can be lethal in VT.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: A haemodynamically stable patient has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 180/min. A modified Valsalva manoeuvre fails. What is the next step?

options.A: Amiodarone 300 mg IV bolus
options.B: Synchronised cardioversion without sedation, starting at 120 J biphasic
options.C: Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push, then 12 mg if unsuccessful
options.D: Digoxin 500 µg IV
options.E: Metoprolol 50 mg IV bolus

explanation: For stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia, vagal manoeuvres are first line; if unsuccessful, adenosine 6 mg is given rapidly into a large vein with a saline flush, followed by 12 mg if needed; ERC 2025 advises considering a further 18 mg dose if the patient tolerates the side effects (AHA 2025 lists 6 mg then 12 mg). Adenosine is avoided when the resting ECG shows pre-excitation. Recording the ECG during adenosine may reveal atrial flutter.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]; ERC 2025 adult ALS [251]
updateNote: Third adenosine dose corrected to 18 mg (ERC 2025 algorithm); text previously said a further 12 mg.

stem: A 25-year-old man has an irregular broad-complex tachycardia at 240/min with varying QRS morphology; he has a known Wolff–Parkinson–White pattern. He is alert, with BP 118/76 mmHg. Which treatment should be avoided?

options.A: Ibutilide
options.B: Synchronised cardioversion under sedation
options.C: Procainamide
options.D: Flecainide in the absence of structural heart disease
options.E: Adenosine

explanation: Pre-excited AF should not be treated with AV-nodal blockers such as adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin or beta-blockers, because they enhance conduction down the accessory pathway and can precipitate VF. Electrical cardioversion is preferred if unstable; procainamide, ibutilide or flecainide are options in stable patients.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]; Van Gelder et al. 2024 (ESC atrial fibrillation) [223]

stem: Routine sodium bicarbonate during cardiac arrest is not recommended. In which situation is it specifically indicated?

options.A: Arrest with an arterial pH of 7.20
options.B: Cardiac arrest from tricyclic antidepressant overdose
options.C: Prolonged VF lasting more than 10 minutes despite three shocks
options.D: Asystole in a patient with sepsis
options.E: PEA arrest after major trauma

explanation: Sodium bicarbonate is not recommended routinely during CPR. It is indicated for life-threatening hyperkalaemia and cardiac arrest from sodium-channel-blocking drugs such as tricyclic antidepressants (50 mmol bolus, targeting serum pH 7.45–7.55). Correcting moderate acidaemia alone does not improve outcomes.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]; Nelson et al. 2019 (Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies) [151]

stem: Immediately after delivering a shock for VF, what should the team do next?

options.A: Give adrenaline before resuming compressions
options.B: Analyse the rhythm immediately and deliver a second shock if VF persists
options.C: Ventilate with 2 breaths, then check the rhythm
options.D: Resume chest compressions immediately without a rhythm or pulse check
options.E: Check for a pulse for 10 seconds

explanation: After each shock, chest compressions should be resumed immediately for 2 minutes without pausing to check the rhythm or pulse, because even after successful defibrillation the heart rarely produces an effective output immediately. Minimising pre- and post-shock pauses improves defibrillation success.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: Which measure of CPR quality is best associated with improved survival and is monitored by many resuscitation teams?

options.A: Chest compression fraction of at least 60%, ideally around 80%
options.B: Pausing CPR for 30 seconds every 2 minutes for a full pulse check
options.C: Ventilation rate of 20 breaths/min
options.D: Rescuer rotation every 10 minutes
options.E: Delivering compressions at 140/min

explanation: The chest compression fraction is the proportion of resuscitation time during which compressions are performed; AHA recommends at least 60%, with 80% achievable. Rescuers should change every 2 minutes to prevent fatigue, and pauses for rhythm checks should be under 10 seconds.
referenceText: Panchal et al. 2020 (AHA adult BLS/ALS) [158]; Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: During a cardiac arrest, two attempts at peripheral IV cannulation fail. What is the recommended alternative route for drug delivery?

options.A: Wait for central venous catheterisation before giving drugs
options.B: Subcutaneous injection
options.C: Endotracheal administration of drugs
options.D: Intraosseous access
options.E: Intracardiac injection of adrenaline

explanation: When IV access is difficult, intraosseous access is the recommended alternative in adults. Endotracheal drug delivery is no longer recommended because absorption is unpredictable, and intracardiac injection is dangerous and interrupts compressions.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: In which scenario is a mechanical chest compression device most reasonable?

options.A: Routine use in all in-hospital cardiac arrests
options.B: Arrest in the first 2 minutes before a defibrillator arrives
options.C: Replacing manual compressions in a well-staffed resuscitation team at the bedside
options.D: Ongoing CPR during transfer for PCI or extracorporeal CPR
options.E: Asystolic arrest with a do-not-resuscitate order

explanation: Trials have not shown superiority of mechanical compression devices over high-quality manual CPR, so routine use is not recommended. They are a reasonable alternative when manual compressions are impractical or unsafe, such as during transport, prolonged CPR, PCI or as a bridge to ECPR.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: Which patient is the most appropriate candidate for extracorporeal CPR (ECPR)?

options.A: A patient with metastatic cancer in PEA arrest
options.B: An 85-year-old with unwitnessed asystole after 40 minutes of CPR in a district hospital
options.C: A patient with severe aortic regurgitation and aortic dissection
options.D: A 45-year-old with witnessed, refractory VF arrest and bystander CPR at an ECMO centre
options.E: A patient with ROSC after 5 minutes of CPR

explanation: ECPR may be considered as a rescue therapy for selected patients with refractory arrest and a potentially reversible cause, especially witnessed arrest with bystander CPR, shockable rhythm, short low-flow time and younger age, in settings where it can be implemented. Unwitnessed asystole, prolonged no-flow time and terminal illness are poor candidates.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: A patient comatose after cardiac arrest develops generalised tonic–clonic seizures on day 1. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Treat the seizures; levetiracetam or valproate are first-line, in addition to sedatives
options.B: Seizures after cardiac arrest should not be treated, because they indicate a poor prognosis
options.C: Phenytoin is the preferred first-line agent
options.D: Seizure prophylaxis should be started in all post-arrest patients
options.E: Neuromuscular blockade alone is sufficient treatment

explanation: ERC–ESICM recommend treating clinical seizures, using levetiracetam or valproate as first-line agents along with sedatives; routine seizure prophylaxis is not recommended. Neuromuscular blockers mask the motor manifestations but do not stop electrical seizure activity, so EEG monitoring is needed.
referenceText: Nolan et al. 2021 (ERC–ESICM post-resuscitation care) [153]

stem: Which blood glucose management strategy is recommended for adults after ROSC?

options.A: Tight glucose control at 4.4–6.1 mmol/L (80–110 mg/dL) using an insulin infusion
options.B: Insulin only if glucose exceeds 25 mmol/L (450 mg/dL)
options.C: Allow glucose up to 20 mmol/L (360 mg/dL) to maintain cerebral substrate
options.D: Routine glucose-containing fluids for 48 hours
options.E: Maintain glucose at 7.8–10 mmol/L (140–180 mg/dL) and avoid hypoglycaemia

explanation: ERC–ESICM follow standard ICU practice: hyperglycaemia above 10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) is treated with insulin while avoiding hypoglycaemia. Intensive insulin therapy (NICE-SUGAR) increased mortality and hypoglycaemia in critically ill patients.
referenceText: Nolan et al. 2021 (ERC–ESICM post-resuscitation care) [153]; NICE-SUGAR Investigators 2009 [152]

stem: A comatose patient after cardiac arrest has a brain CT at 24 hours. Which finding most strongly supports severe hypoxic–ischaemic brain injury?

options.A: Normal CT appearance
options.B: Mild cerebral atrophy appropriate for age
options.C: Diffuse cerebral oedema with a reduced grey-to-white matter ratio
options.D: Sinus mucosal thickening
options.E: A small old lacunar infarct in the left internal capsule, unchanged from 2019

explanation: Hypoxic–ischaemic brain injury on CT appears as diffuse oedema with loss of grey–white differentiation (reduced grey-to-white matter ratio, GWR) and sulcal effacement, typically within 72 h. It is one of the multimodal predictors in the ERC–ESICM algorithm; MRI with diffusion restriction is also used.
referenceText: Nolan et al. 2021 (ERC–ESICM post-resuscitation care) [153]

stem: During an in-hospital arrest, which factor is the most appropriate basis for deciding to stop resuscitation?

options.A: A single ETCO2 reading of 8 mmHg at 2 minutes after intubation, even if compressions were poor
options.B: Pupils dilated and fixed after 5 minutes of CPR
options.C: Asystole persisting after 20 minutes of ALS with no reversible cause, hypothermia or toxin
options.D: Failure to achieve ROSC after the first shock
options.E: Age over 80 years alone

explanation: Stopping CPR is considered when asystole persists for more than 20 minutes of ALS in the absence of a reversible cause. Low ETCO2 should not be used in isolation, especially early in CPR, and pupil size is unreliable during arrest. Hypothermia and drug intoxication are reasons to continue.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: A woman 3 days after hip surgery collapses with PEA. Bedside echocardiography during the pulse check shows a dilated right ventricle, and massive PE is strongly suspected. What is the most appropriate intervention?

options.A: Insert an inferior vena cava filter
options.B: Give thrombolysis and consider continuing CPR for 60–90 minutes after administration
options.C: Perform pericardiocentesis
options.D: Avoid thrombolysis because of recent surgery, and stop CPR after 20 minutes without ROSC
options.E: Give unfractionated heparin alone and wait for CT pulmonary angiography

explanation: In cardiac arrest from suspected PE, thrombolysis is recommended; recent surgery is a relative contraindication that is outweighed by imminent death. CPR should be continued for 60–90 minutes after administering thrombolytics; surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy are alternatives.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]; Konstantinides et al. 2020 (ESC pulmonary embolism) [117]

stem: A known heroin user is found pulseless and apnoeic. What is the most important initial intervention?

options.A: Naloxone 0.4 mg intramuscularly only, without CPR
options.B: High-quality CPR and ventilation per standard ALS; naloxone is not the priority
options.C: Naloxone 2 mg IV first, then wait 2 minutes for a response before starting CPR
options.D: Flumazenil 0.5 mg IV
options.E: Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg IV

explanation: In opioid-associated cardiac arrest, standard BLS/ALS with high-quality CPR and ventilation take priority; there is no evidence that naloxone improves outcome once the patient is pulseless. Naloxone is useful for opioid-induced respiratory arrest with a pulse.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]; Panchal et al. 2020 (AHA adult BLS/ALS) [158]

stem: A patient has complete heart block with broad QRS escape at 30/min, BP 70/40 mmHg and confusion. Atropine 500 µg IV twice has had no effect. What is the next step?

options.A: Observe closely, because complete heart block rarely causes haemodynamic compromise
options.B: Increase atropine to 6 mg
options.C: Amiodarone 300 mg IV
options.D: Adenosine 6 mg IV
options.E: Transcutaneous pacing or adrenaline infusion as a bridge to transvenous pacing

explanation: In unstable bradycardia unresponsive to atropine (up to 3 mg), ERC recommends interim measures such as isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion and transcutaneous pacing while arranging transvenous pacing. Broad-complex escape rhythms are unstable and carry a risk of asystole.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: A patient develops anaphylaxis after IV antibiotic and becomes pulseless. What is the correct adrenaline administration?

options.A: Adrenaline 5 mg IV bolus
options.B: A single dose of adrenaline 0.1 mg IV, then antihistamines and hydrocortisone
options.C: Adrenaline 1 mg IV every 3–5 minutes per standard ALS, plus a rapid fluid bolus
options.D: Adrenaline 0.5 mg intramuscularly every 5 minutes only
options.E: Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV instead of adrenaline

explanation: Before arrest, IM adrenaline 0.5 mg is first line in anaphylaxis. Once in cardiac arrest, standard ALS doses of IV adrenaline (1 mg every 3–5 minutes) apply, together with rapid IV crystalloid. Antihistamines and steroids are not resuscitation drugs.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]; Cardona et al. 2020 (WAO anaphylaxis guidance) [30]

stem: A patient after cardiac arrest is undergoing active fever prevention with a surface cooling device and develops vigorous shivering. Which intervention is appropriate?

options.A: Optimise sedation and analgesia, adding magnesium, counter-warming or neuromuscular blockade
options.B: Give paracetamol 4 g IV as a single bolus and increase the cooling device setting
options.C: Stop temperature control
options.D: Give flumazenil
options.E: Increase the cooling intensity to reach 30 °C so that the shivering threshold is passed quickly

explanation: Shivering increases metabolic rate, oxygen consumption and heat production. It is managed in a stepwise fashion with sedation and opioids, magnesium, skin counter-warming, dexmedetomidine or meperidine, and neuromuscular blockade if refractory. Cooling below 32 °C increases arrhythmias and coagulopathy.
referenceText: Nolan et al. 2021 (ERC–ESICM post-resuscitation care) [153]

stem: Which statement regarding point-of-care ultrasound during cardiac arrest is most accurate?

options.A: It can identify reversible causes such as tamponade, but pauses must not exceed 10 seconds
options.B: It is contraindicated during CPR
options.C: Probe placement and full image acquisition should occur during a dedicated 30-second pause in CPR
options.D: It should replace capnography for confirming tube placement
options.E: Cardiac standstill alone is sufficient to stop resuscitation

explanation: Ultrasound can identify tamponade, pneumothorax, RV dilatation in PE or hypovolaemia, but it should be performed by skilled operators during the brief rhythm check with minimal interruption. Cardiac standstill should not be used in isolation to terminate resuscitation; subcostal views prolong pauses if done incorrectly.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: When using a biphasic defibrillator in an adult VF arrest, what is the recommended energy for the first shock?

options.A: 50 J for the first shock, increasing by 50 J for each subsequent shock
options.B: At least 150 J (or according to the manufacturer's guidance)
options.C: 360 J only if monophasic
options.D: 100 J with no escalation
options.E: 10 J/kg

explanation: ERC 2021 recommends a first biphasic shock of at least 150 J, with escalation (e.g. to 200 J or higher) if the first shock fails or VF recurs, according to the device. Monophasic devices deliver 360 J. Weight-based dosing applies to children.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: A patient in the CCU has had six episodes of VT requiring defibrillation within 2 hours despite amiodarone. Which intervention is most likely to reduce recurrence?

options.A: Isoprenaline infusion
options.B: Stopping all antiarrhythmic drugs to unmask the underlying rhythm
options.C: Adenosine 12 mg IV
options.D: Deep sedation and beta-blockade, considering catheter ablation
options.E: Flecainide IV bolus

explanation: Electrical storm (three or more episodes of sustained VT/VF in 24 hours) is driven by sympathetic activation. Management includes sedation, beta-blockers (e.g. propranolol or esmolol), amiodarone, correction of electrolytes and ischaemia, and catheter ablation; mechanical circulatory support may be needed.
referenceText: Zeppenfeld et al. 2022 (ESC ventricular arrhythmias) [246]; Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: A nurse finds a patient unresponsive with agonal gasping in a hospital corridor. What is the most appropriate interpretation and action?

options.A: Gasping indicates adequate respiration; place the patient in the recovery position and observe
options.B: Agonal gasping is a sign of cardiac arrest; call for help and start CPR immediately
options.C: Check for a carotid pulse for 30 seconds before deciding
options.D: Wait for the arrest team before starting compressions
options.E: Give 2 rescue breaths and reassess in 2 minutes

explanation: Agonal breathing is common in the first minutes of cardiac arrest and should not be confused with normal breathing. Absence of normal breathing in an unresponsive patient should prompt immediate CPR and a call for help; pulse checks are unreliable and should not take more than 10 seconds.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: A patient with severe hypoxic–ischaemic brain injury after cardiac arrest does not fulfil death by neurological criteria, and the family and team decide on withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment. What is the appropriate approach to organ donation?

options.A: Consider controlled donation after circulatory death, with the withdrawal decision made independently
options.B: Donation is not possible unless brain death criteria are met
options.C: Donation teams should decide the timing of withdrawal
options.D: Donation after circulatory death is unethical, because the organs are always damaged by warm ischaemia
options.E: Organ donation should be discussed before any prognostic assessment

explanation: ERC–ESICM recommend that all patients with poor prognosis after cardiac arrest be considered for organ donation (after brain death or controlled circulatory death). The decision to withdraw life-sustaining treatment must be made independently of the donation process to avoid conflicts of interest.
referenceText: Nolan et al. 2021 (ERC–ESICM post-resuscitation care) [153]; Greer et al. 2020 (World Brain Death Project) [83]

stem: Which list correctly includes the four "Ts" among the reversible causes of cardiac arrest?

options.A: Tamponade, tachyphylaxis, trauma, thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary)
options.B: Tension pneumothorax, tetany, toxins, temperature
options.C: Tachycardia, tamponade, trauma, toxins
options.D: Thyroid storm, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis
options.E: Tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis

explanation: The ERC lists the 4 Hs (hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo-/hyperkalaemia and other metabolic disorders, hypo-/hyperthermia) and 4 Ts (thrombosis – coronary or pulmonary, tension pneumothorax, tamponade – cardiac, and toxins). Systematic exclusion improves the chance of ROSC.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: A patient develops PEA 2 hours after cardiac surgery. Echocardiography shows a pericardial collection compressing the right heart. What is the definitive management?

options.A: Emergency resternotomy
options.B: Needle pericardiocentesis followed by observation
options.C: Thrombolysis
options.D: Large-volume fluid bolus only
options.E: Increase PEEP

explanation: Post-cardiotomy tamponade causing arrest is managed by emergency resternotomy, which should be performed within about 5 minutes if there is no ROSC. Clots are often loculated, making needle pericardiocentesis less effective than in medical tamponade.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]

stem: For a ventilated post-cardiac-arrest patient without ARDS, which ventilation strategy is recommended?

options.A: Lung-protective ventilation with tidal volume of 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight
options.B: High-frequency oscillatory ventilation
options.C: Tidal volume of 12 mL/kg predicted body weight to prevent atelectasis and hypercapnia
options.D: Hyperventilation to PaCO2 of 25 mmHg to reduce intracranial pressure
options.E: Zero PEEP to maximise cerebral venous drainage

explanation: ERC–ESICM recommend lung-protective ventilation with tidal volumes of 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, adequate PEEP and normocapnia after ROSC. Routine hyperventilation risks cerebral ischaemia; HFOV is not recommended.
referenceText: Nolan et al. 2021 (ERC–ESICM post-resuscitation care) [153]; ARDS Network 2000 (ARMA low tidal volume) [207]

stem: During intubation in the ICU, a patient desaturates to 60% and develops bradycardia followed by PEA. Which is the most important initial action?

options.A: Wait 2 minutes for spontaneous recovery
options.B: Give atropine 3 mg and continue the laryngoscopy
options.C: Start CPR and reoxygenate with 100% oxygen via facemask or supraglottic airway
options.D: Give sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol
options.E: Continue intubation attempts until successful, deferring CPR until the airway is secured

explanation: Hypoxia is a major reversible cause of peri-intubation arrest. CPR must be started immediately and oxygenation restored by the simplest effective technique (bag-mask, supraglottic airway, or front-of-neck access in a CICO situation). Prolonged laryngoscopy attempts without oxygenation worsen hypoxia.
referenceText: Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]; Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

stem: Why is early withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment within 72 hours of ROSC discouraged when it is based solely on neurological prognosis?

options.A: Clinical examination is more reliable at 24 hours than at 72 hours, so early decisions are safer
options.B: Organ function always recovers fully by 72 hours
options.C: Biomarkers are only measurable after 72 hours
options.D: Sedation and temperature control confound examination, risking a self-fulfilling prophecy
options.E: Legal regulations require 7 days of support

explanation: Withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy based on early neurological examination risks self-fulfilling prophecies, especially given confounding by sedatives, hypothermia and organ dysfunction. ERC–ESICM 2025 advise considering prognostication at 72 hours or later after ROSC in patients not obeying commands (GCS motor score below 6), using a multimodal approach with two or more concordant predictors; some tests (SSEP from 24 h, EEG after 24 h) can be recorded earlier but are interpreted within this framework.
referenceText: Nolan et al. 2021 (ERC–ESICM post-resuscitation care) [153]; ERC–ESICM 2025 post-resuscitation care [249]
updateNote: ERC–ESICM 2025 prognostication timing and GCS motor <6 criterion.

stem: What did the PARAMEDIC2 trial show about adrenaline use in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?

options.A: Adrenaline improved both 30-day survival and survival with favourable neurological outcome significantly
options.B: Adrenaline reduced survival compared with placebo
options.C: High-dose adrenaline improved neurological outcomes
options.D: Adrenaline improved 30-day survival, without significant improvement in favourable neurological outcome
options.E: Adrenaline had no effect on ROSC

explanation: PARAMEDIC2 randomised OHCA patients to adrenaline or placebo; adrenaline increased ROSC and 30-day survival, but the difference in survival with favourable neurological outcome was not significant, and more survivors on adrenaline had severe neurological impairment. ERC still recommends adrenaline in ALS.
referenceText: Perkins et al. 2018 (PARAMEDIC2) [165]; Soar et al. 2021 (ERC adult ALS) [200]
